claim: Primary cortical areas contain maps of sensory features, including sound frequency in primary auditory cortex (A1).

claim: Two-photon calcium imaging in mice has confirmed the presence of global tonotopic maps in A1.
source: Two-photon calcium imaging in mice has confirmed the presence of these global tonotopic maps, while uncovering an unexpected local variability in the stimulus preferences of individual neurons in A1 and other primary regions.
evidence: This statement references prior research findings using two-photon imaging in mice.

claim: Two-photon calcium imaging in mice has uncovered unexpected local variability in the stimulus preferences of individual neurons in A1 and other primary regions.

claim: Local variance in frequency preferences is equivalent in ferrets and mice.
source: Using two-photon calcium imaging in layers 2/3, we found that local variance in frequency preferences is equivalent in ferrets and mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data comparing ferrets and mice.

claim: Neurons with multipeaked frequency tuning are less spatially organized than those tuned to a single frequency in both ferrets and mice.

claim: Microelectrode recordings may describe a smoother tonotopic arrangement due to a sampling bias towards neurons with simple frequency tuning.
source: Furthermore, we show that microelectrode recordings may describe a smoother tonotopic arrangement due to a sampling bias towards neurons with simple frequency tuning.
evidence: This is a finding of the study based on comparison of two-photon imaging and microelectrode recording data.

claim: More recent multielectrode recordings have confirmed the presence of a tonotopic gradient over large areas of A1 in carnivores and primates.
source: More recent multielectrode recordings (Imaizumi et al., 2004; Bizley et al., 2005; Recanzone et al., 1999) and large-scale imaging experiments (Nelken et al., 2008) have confirmed the presence of a tonotopic gradient over large areas of A1 in carnivores and primates, while single-neuron recordings in awake animals have reported clear frequency gradients in marmosets (Bendor and Wang, 2008) and weaker tonotopy in cats (Goldstein et al., 1970).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Large-scale imaging experiments have confirmed the presence of a tonotopic gradient over large areas of A1 in carnivores and primates.

claim: In vivo two-photon calcium imaging can measure the stimulus preferences of a much larger number of individual neurons within a cortical region than multielectrode recordings and large-scale imaging.
source: In vivo two-photon calcium imaging can measure the stimulus preferences of a much larger number of individual neurons within a cortical region than the above techniques, improving the spatial sampling of mapping studies.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of two-photon imaging based on established knowledge.

claim: Previous electrophysiological and large-scale imaging studies confirmed an overall tonotopic organization in mouse A1.
source: While previous electrophysiological and large-scale imaging studies confirmed an overall tonotopic organization in mouse A1 (Hackett et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2012; Stiebler et al., 1997), more recent two-photon imaging studies have reported different degrees of frequency tuning variability among neighboring neurons, from well-ordered local maps (Issa et al., 2014) to moderately heterogeneous tuning (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2010; Rothschild et al., 2010; Panniello et al., 2018; Romero et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: More recent two-photon imaging studies have reported different degrees of frequency tuning variability among neighboring neurons in mouse A1, from well-ordered local maps to moderately heterogeneous tuning.
source: While previous electrophysiological and large-scale imaging studies confirmed an overall tonotopic organization in mouse A1 (Hackett et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2012; Stiebler et al., 1997), more recent two-photon imaging studies have reported different degrees of frequency tuning variability among neighboring neurons, from well-ordered local maps (Issa et al., 2014) to moderately heterogeneous tuning (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2010; Rothschild et al., 2010; Panniello et al., 2018; Romero et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Two-photon imaging has revealed local heterogeneity in whisker selectivity in mouse primary somatosensory cortex.
source: Similarly, two-photon imaging has revealed local heterogeneity in whisker selectivity in mouse primary somatosensory cortex (Kerr et al., 2007; Sato et al., 2007), and in orientation tuning in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) (Bonin et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Two-photon imaging has revealed local heterogeneity in orientation tuning in mouse primary visual cortex (V1).

claim: Microelectrode studies are often based on responses that are summed across several neurons, and this spatial averaging may lead to smoother tonotopic gradients.
source: Microelectrode studies are often based on responses that are summed across several neurons, and this spatial averaging may lead to smoother tonotopic gradients (Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents an inference about methodological effects.

claim: In single neuron recordings, the spacing between cells is at least 50 μm and typically ~100 μm or greater.
source: Even in single neuron recordings, the spacing between cells is at least 50 μm (South and Weinberger, 1995), and typically ~100 μm or greater, so variations in stimulus preferences between neighboring cells are not usually examined (Kanold et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Studies investigating layers 2/3 and 4 have usually found smoother tonotopy in the deeper layers.
source: Studies investigating layers 2/3 and 4 have usually found smoother tonotopy in the deeper layers (Guo et al., 2012; Winkowski and Kanold, 2013) (but see Tischbirek et al., 2019, reporting similar tonotopic organization across all layers of mouse auditory cortex).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Local thalamic inputs to A1 in mice are heterogeneous in their frequency tuning.
source: The variations in tonotopy across studies may also partly reflect a species difference in the cortical organization of rodents and higher mammals, particularly as local thalamic inputs to A1 in mice are also heterogeneous in their frequency tuning (Vasquez-Lopez et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Two-photon imaging studies of primary visual cortex have revealed poorer spatial organization of orientation tuning in rodents than in cats.
source: Two-photon imaging studies of primary visual cortex have revealed poorer spatial organization of orientation tuning in rodents than in cats (Bonin et al., 2011; Ohki et al., 2005), tree shrews (Lee et al., 2016), and ferrets (Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Two-photon imaging studies of primary visual cortex have revealed poorer spatial organization of orientation tuning in rodents than in tree shrews.

claim: A1 in marmosets was reported to be more tonotopically organized than in rats.
source: This view is supported by a recent study in marmosets, in which A1 was reported to be more tonotopically organized than in rats (Zeng et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Throughout the ascending auditory pathway, neurons progressively integrate spectral and temporal features of sound.
source: Throughout the ascending auditory pathway, neurons progressively integrate spectral and temporal features of sound (Linden and Schreiner, 2003), and the receptive fields of many A1 neurons are poorly predicted by a model of linear tuning to a single sound frequency (Ahrens et al., 2008; Sadagopan and Wang, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The receptive fields of many A1 neurons are poorly predicted by a model of linear tuning to a single sound frequency.
source: Throughout the ascending auditory pathway, neurons progressively integrate spectral and temporal features of sound (Linden and Schreiner, 2003), and the receptive fields of many A1 neurons are poorly predicted by a model of linear tuning to a single sound frequency (Ahrens et al., 2008; Sadagopan and Wang, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recent studies have shown that the preferred frequencies of A1 neurons with irregular tuning curves are poorly mapped.

claim: Ferrets have a gyrencephalic cortex.
source: Ferrets are a popular animal model in auditory neuroscience because they have a gyrencephalic cortex, their A1 is easily accessible, they are readily trained on behavioural tasks, and (unlike mice) their hearing range overlaps well with the human audiogram (Nodal and King, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge about ferret anatomy.

claim: Neuronal calcium transients were recorded in 3604 neurons across 32 imaging fields in ferrets.
source: We used an AAV vector to express either GCaMP6m (four subjects) or GCaMP6f (four subjects) in the right A1 of ferrets (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B) and recorded neuronal calcium transients in 3604 neurons across 32 imaging fields (e.g. Figure 1A,B), while presenting pure tones (0.3–41 kHz; 30–90 dB SPL) to the contralateral ear.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collected in the study.

claim: Pure tones (0.3–41 kHz; 30–90 dB SPL) were presented to the contralateral ear during ferret recordings.
source: We used an AAV vector to express either GCaMP6m (four subjects) or GCaMP6f (four subjects) in the right A1 of ferrets (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B) and recorded neuronal calcium transients in 3604 neurons across 32 imaging fields (e.g. Figure 1A,B), while presenting pure tones (0.3–41 kHz; 30–90 dB SPL) to the contralateral ear.

claim: Neuronal activity was imaged at 176 ± 26.83 μm (median ± SD) below the cortical surface in ferrets.

claim: 693 of 3604 (19.23%) neurons in ferret A1 were frequency-sensitive.
source: Across all fields imaged in ferret A1, 693 of 3604 (19.23%) neurons were frequency-sensitive (two-way ANOVA; p<0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: In the example field shown in Figure 1, 26.5% of neurons were significantly sensitive to tone frequency or frequency/level combinations.
source: In the example field shown in Figure 1 (300 × 300 µm), 26.5% of neurons were significantly sensitive to tone frequency or frequency/level combinations, and the average BF across all frequency-sensitive neurons (Figure 1C) was 14.7 kHz (±0.75 kHz; mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data for a specific example.

claim: The average BF across all frequency-sensitive neurons in the example field shown in Figure 1 was 14.7 kHz (±0.75 kHz; mean ± SEM).

evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data for a specific example.

claim: Most neurons within a local region of ferret A1 were tuned to a similar BF, but there were some outliers preferring higher or lower BFs.
source: As previously described for A1 of mice (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2010; Rothschild et al., 2010; Panniello et al., 2018), most neurons within this local region of ferret A1 were tuned to a similar BF, but there were some outliers preferring higher or lower BFs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the experimental data, supported by citations to similar findings in mice.

claim: The BF of individual neurons in the example field ranged from 2.2 kHz to 19.9 kHz, with 9% of BFs being more than one octave away from the mean.

claim: Best frequencies varied less within an imaging field among single-peaked neurons (1.34 ± 0.10 octaves; mean ± SEM) than among double-peaked neurons (2.16 ± 0.18 octaves).
source: Best frequencies varied less within an imaging field among single-peaked neurons (1.34 ± 0.10 octaves; mean ± SEM) than among double-peaked neurons (2.16 ± 0.18 octaves; t-test: t = −4.15, p=4.1×10−5) and complex neurons (3.05 ± 0.24 octaves; t = 7.55, p=3.4×10−13) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: Best frequencies varied less within an imaging field among single-peaked neurons (1.34 ± 0.10 octaves; mean ± SEM) than among complex neurons (3.05 ± 0.24 octaves).
source: Best frequencies varied less within an imaging field among single-peaked neurons (1.34 ± 0.10 octaves; mean ± SEM) than among double-peaked neurons (2.16 ± 0.18 octaves; t-test: t = −4.15, p=4.1×10−5) and complex neurons (3.05 ± 0.24 octaves; t = 7.55, p=3.4×10−13) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: The average deconvolved calcium response at the best frequency and level combination was stronger in single-peaked neurons compared to either double-peaked neurons or neurons with complex FRAs.
source: We found that the average deconvolved calcium response at the best frequency and level combination was stronger in single-peaked neurons compared to either double-peaked neurons (t-test: t = 2.22, p=0.027) or neurons with complex FRAs (t = 4.02, p=6.9×10−5).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: There was no significant difference in response strength between neurons with double-peaked and complex FRAs.
source: There was no significant difference in response strength between neurons with double-peaked and complex FRAs (t = 1.58, p=0.11).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: The Fano Factor calculated at the best frequency and level did not significantly differ between neurons in the three FRA classes.
source: The Fano Factor calculated at the best frequency and level did not significantly differ between neurons in the three FRA classes (single- and double-peaked: t = 0.60, p=0.55; single-peaked and complex: t = 0.638, p=0.52), indicating that responses at BF were equally reliable for neurons with single- and multi-peaked FRAs (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: A higher percentage of frequency-sensitive neurons was found in the GCaMP6m (32.29%) compared to the GCaMP6f dataset (10.81%).
source: As expected, when data from GCaMP6m and GCaMP6f injections were analyzed separately, we found a higher percentage of frequency-sensitive neurons in the GCaMP6m (32.29%), compared to the GCaMP6f dataset (10.81%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data comparing two calcium indicators.

claim: Both GCaMP6m and GCaMP6f indicators showed similar effects of FRA class on local BF variance, response strength and response reliability.
source: Importantly, both indicators showed similar effects of FRA class on local BF variance, response strength and response reliability (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), so our main findings are consistent across the two indicators, and data are pooled across all ferrets for our remaining analyses.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data comparing two calcium indicators.

claim: The microelectrode recordings yielded a higher proportion of neurons with single-peaked FRAs than the imaging experiments.
source: Although all three FRA classes were observed, the microelectrode recordings yielded a higher proportion of neurons with single-peaked FRAs (Likelihood Ratio Test: χ2 = 68.45, p=1.1×10−16) than the imaging experiments, and fewer with double-peaked (χ2 = 22.16, p=2.5×10−6) and complex (χ2 = 30.06, p=4.2×10−8) FRAs (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing two experimental methods with statistical testing.

claim: The microelectrode recordings yielded fewer neurons with double-peaked FRAs than the imaging experiments.

claim: The microelectrode recordings yielded fewer neurons with complex FRAs than the imaging experiments.

claim: In microelectrode recordings, there was no significant difference between the spike rates of neurons with single- and double-peaked FRAs.
source: Contrary to our two-photon imaging results, we did not find a significant difference between the spike rates of neurons with single- and double-peaked FRAs (t-test: t = 1.29, p=0.20) or between those with single-peaked and complex FRAs (t = 0.05, p=0.96) in our microelectrode recordings (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the microelectrode recording data with statistical testing.

claim: In microelectrode recordings, there was no significant difference between the spike rates of neurons with single-peaked and complex FRAs.
source: Contrary to our two-photon imaging results, we did not find a significant difference between the spike rates of neurons with single- and double-peaked FRAs (t-test: t = 1.29, p=0.20) or between those with single-peaked and complex FRAs (t = 0.05, p=0.96) in our microelectrode recordings (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).

claim: Signal correlations differed across the three FRA classes (single-peaked, double-peaked, and complex).

claim: Signal correlations within complex neurons (0.048 ± 0.003; mean ± SEM) were significantly lower than those for single-peaked (0.207 ± 0.002) and double-peaked neurons (0.193 ± 0.002).
source: In post hoc pairwise tests (Tukey's HSD), signal correlations within complex neurons (0.048 ± 0.003; mean ± SEM) were significantly lower than those for single-peaked (0.207 ± 0.002; p=9.6×10−10) and double-peaked neurons (0.193 ± 0.002; p=9.6×10−10).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: Signal correlations were significantly higher within single-peaked neurons than double-peaked neurons.

evidence: This is a result from the experimental data with reference to figures.

claim: When single-peaked neurons were projected onto a global A1 template, the expected tonotopic gradient was clearly evident.
source: When single-peaked neurons were projected onto this global A1 template, the expected tonotopic gradient was clearly evident (Figure 4A1), with high frequencies mapped onto the dorsal tip of the ectosylvian gyrus (Figure 4B1) and lower frequencies toward the ventral border with secondary posterior fields (Kelly et al., 1986a; Bizley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data with reference to figures and citations.

claim: High frequencies are mapped onto the dorsal tip of the ectosylvian gyrus in ferret A1.
source: When single-peaked neurons were projected onto this global A1 template, the expected tonotopic gradient was clearly evident (Figure 4A1), with high frequencies mapped onto the dorsal tip of the ectosylvian gyrus (Figure 4B1) and lower frequencies toward the ventral border with secondary posterior fields (Kelly et al., 1986a; Bizley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data with reference to figures and citations.

claim: Lower frequencies are mapped toward the ventral border with secondary posterior fields in ferret A1.
source: When single-peaked neurons were projected onto this global A1 template, the expected tonotopic gradient was clearly evident (Figure 4A1), with high frequencies mapped onto the dorsal tip of the ectosylvian gyrus (Figure 4B1) and lower frequencies toward the ventral border with secondary posterior fields (Kelly et al., 1986a; Bizley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data with reference to figures and citations.

claim: The large-scale spatial organization of frequency preferences along the tonotopic gradient showed a correlation between BFs and the neuron's position along the tonotopic axis (r = −0.40, p=1.1×10−12) for single-peaked neurons.
source: The large-scale spatial organization of frequency preferences along the tonotopic gradient was quantified as a correlation between BFs and the neuron's position along the tonotopic axis (Pearson's correlation: r = −0.40, p=1.1×10−12; Figure 4C1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: When examining only neurons with double-peaked FRAs (BFd), global tonotopy was clearly visible and statistically significant (r = 0.46, p=5.7×10−13).
source: When examining only neurons with double-peaked FRAs (BFd), global tonotopy was clearly visible (Figure 4A2, B2), and this tonotopic gradient was again statistically significant (r = 0.46, p=5.7×10−13; Figure 4C2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: The BFs of double-peaked neurons varied more around their fitted tonotopic gradient than those of single-peaked neurons.
source: However, the BFs of double-peaked neurons varied more around their fitted tonotopic gradient (red line, Figure 4C2) than those of single-peaked neurons (t-test: t = 2.43, p=0.02), suggesting that neurons with double-peaked FRAs have a less smooth tonotopic organization.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: The BFs of neurons with complex FRAs were organized tonotopically on the global A1 template (r = 0.32, p=1.8×10−5).
source: The BFs of neurons with complex FRAs were also organized tonotopically on the global A1 template (r = 0.32, p=1.8×10−5; Figure 4A4, B4), but were more variable around the tonotopic gradient (Figure 4C4) than the BFs of either single-peaked (t = 6.83, p=2.7×10−11) or double-peaked (t = 4.52, p=8.2×10−6) neurons.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: The BFs of neurons with complex FRAs were more variable around the tonotopic gradient than the BFs of either single-peaked or double-peaked neurons.
source: The BFs of neurons with complex FRAs were also organized tonotopically on the global A1 template (r = 0.32, p=1.8×10−5; Figure 4A4, B4), but were more variable around the tonotopic gradient (Figure 4C4) than the BFs of either single-peaked (t = 6.83, p=2.7×10−11) or double-peaked (t = 4.52, p=8.2×10−6) neurons.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: The frequency of the second-strongest peak of double-peaked FRAs (peak 2) did not change systematically along the tonotopic axis (r = −0.096, p=0.15).
source: In contrast to BF, other aspects of the neurons' frequency responses were not found to be systematically ordered along the tonotopic gradient. The frequency of the second-strongest peak of double-peaked FRAs (peak 2) did not change systematically along this axis (r = −0.096, p=0.15; Figure 4A3, B3, C3), nor did the differences between the two peaks of double-peaked neurons (r = 0.13, p=0.046; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: The differences between the two peaks of double-peaked neurons did not change systematically along the tonotopic axis (r = 0.13, p=0.046).
source: In contrast to BF, other aspects of the neurons' frequency responses were not found to be systematically ordered along the tonotopic gradient. The frequency of the second-strongest peak of double-peaked FRAs (peak 2) did not change systematically along this axis (r = −0.096, p=0.15; Figure 4A3, B3, C3), nor did the differences between the two peaks of double-peaked neurons (r = 0.13, p=0.046; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: Neuropil signal introduced the appearance of a tonotopic order to the second peaks of double-peaked neurons.
source: For example, we found that neuropil signal introduced the appearance of a tonotopic order to an otherwise spatially disorganized signal – namely, the second peaks of double-peaked neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 4D3).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data comparing neuropil-corrected and uncorrected signals.

claim: 854 of 1964 (43.75%) neurons were frequency-sensitive in mice.
source: Across all imaging fields, 854 of 1964 (43.75%) neurons were frequency-sensitive in mice (two-way ANOVA; p<0.05), while only 693 of 3604 (19.23%) neurons were frequency-sensitive using the same statistical criterion in ferrets.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data in mice.

claim: A higher percentage of frequency-sensitive neurons in the mouse (60.54%) showed 'simpler' frequency receptive fields with a single peak at BF than in the ferret (42.71%).
source: Specifically, a higher percentage of frequency-sensitive neurons in the mouse (60.54%) showed 'simpler' frequency receptive fields with a single peak at BF than in the ferret (42.71%; Likelihood Ratio Test: χ2 = 48.96, p=2.6×10−12).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing mice and ferrets with statistical testing.

claim: Ferrets had more double-peaked (31.75% vs 26.23%) and complex FRAs (24.96% vs. 13.23%) than mice.
source: Conversely, ferrets had more double-peaked (31.75% vs 26.23%; χ2 = 5.67, p=0.017) and complex FRAs (24.96% vs. 13.23%; χ2 = 34.83, p=3.6×10−9) than mice.
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing mice and ferrets with statistical testing.

claim: Single-peaked and double-peaked neurons in mice responded more strongly at BF than complex neurons.
source: Single-peaked and double-peaked neurons in mice responded more strongly at BF than complex neurons (single- and double-peaked: t = −0.73, p=0.46; single-peaked and complex: t = 3.20, p=0.0010; double-peaked and complex: t = 3.43, p=1.9×10−4; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and trial-to-trial reliability in complex neurons was better than that of single-peaked neurons (single- and double-peaked: t = −0.99, p=0.32; single-peaked and complex: t = 2.37, p=0.018; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data in mice with statistical testing.

claim: Trial-to-trial reliability in complex neurons was better than that of single-peaked neurons in mice.
source: Single-peaked and double-peaked neurons in mice responded more strongly at BF than complex neurons (single- and double-peaked: t = −0.73, p=0.46; single-peaked and complex: t = 3.20, p=0.0010; double-peaked and complex: t = 3.43, p=1.9×10−4; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and trial-to-trial reliability in complex neurons was better than that of single-peaked neurons (single- and double-peaked: t = −0.99, p=0.32; single-peaked and complex: t = 2.37, p=0.018; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data in mice with statistical testing.

claim: Neurons with single-peaked FRAs showed broader frequency tuning in mice (0.91 ± 0.03 octaves) compared to ferrets (0.74 ± 0.03 octaves).
source: Neurons with single-peaked FRAs showed broader frequency tuning in mice (0.91 ± 0.03 octaves) compared to ferrets (0.74 ± 0.03 octaves; t-test: t = 3.66, p=2.7×10−4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing mice and ferrets with statistical testing.

claim: There were no significant species differences in tuning bandwidth for double-peaked or complex neurons.
source: However, there were no significant species differences in tuning bandwidth for double-peaked (t = 0.76, p=0.44) or complex neurons (t = 0.72, p=0.47; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing mice and ferrets with statistical testing.

claim: In mice, the BF variability of double-peaked neurons (2.73 ± 0.33 oct/mm; mean ± SEM) was not significantly higher than that of single-peaked neurons (2.57 ± 0.16 oct/mm).
source: Unlike in ferrets, the BF variability of double-peaked neurons (2.73 ± 0.33 oct/mm; mean ± SEM) was not significantly higher than that of single-peaked neurons (2.57 ± 0.16 oct/mm; t-test: t = 0.46, p=0.64) in mice, and the BF variability of the two peaks of double-peaked neurons did not differ significantly (t = 1.15, p=0.25).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data in mice with statistical testing.

claim: In mice, the BFs of neurons with complex FRAs (4.14 ± 0.38 oct/mm) were more variable than those of single-peaked and double-peaked neurons.
source: In line with our ferret data, however, the BFs of neurons with complex FRAs (4.14 ± 0.38 oct/mm) were more variable than those of single-peaked (t = 4.33, p=2.0×10−5) and double-peaked (t = 2.78, p=0.0060) neurons, suggesting that the frequency preferences of neurons with more complex FRAs are less tonotopically organized within the local microcircuit.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data in mice with statistical testing.

claim: The BFs of single-peaked neurons were more variable within a millimetre of A1 in mice (2.18 ± 0.08 octave/mm) than in ferrets (1.33 ± 0.09).
source: The BFs of single-peaked neurons were more variable within a millimetre of A1 in mice (2.18 ± 0.08 octave/mm) than in ferrets (1.33 ± 0.09; t-test: t = 5.62, p=2.5×10−8).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing mice and ferrets with statistical testing.

claim: The percentage of neurons with a BF within the expected range varied across the three different FRA classes but not between species.
source: The resulting values varied across the three different FRA classes (two-way ANOVA: F = 8.41, p=4.3×10−4), but not between species (F = 3.72, p=0.057), and there was no significant interaction between FRA class and species (F = 1.66, p=0.19).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing mice and ferrets with statistical testing.

claim: Post hoc pairwise tests found no significant differences between BF variability in mice and ferrets for single-peaked, double-peaked, or complex neurons.
source: Furthermore, post hoc pairwise Tukey's HSD tests found no significant differences between BF variability in mice and ferrets for single-peaked (p=0.97), double-peaked (p=0.12), or complex neurons (p=1.0).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing mice and ferrets with statistical testing.

claim: Mice and ferrets have equivalent local heterogeneity in frequency preferences within each FRA class of neurons in layers 2/3 of primary auditory cortex.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that mice and ferrets have equivalent local heterogeneity in frequency preferences within each FRA class of neurons in layers 2/3 of primary auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing mice and ferrets.

claim: More complex frequency tuning is associated with more variance in the frequency preferences of neighboring neurons in both mice and ferrets.
source: More complex frequency tuning is associated with more variance in the frequency preferences of neighboring neurons in both species.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in both species.

claim: Ferret A1 shares the same spatial organization as mouse A1, with global tonotopy and local variability.
source: Previous studies in mice have described global A1 tonotopy with local variability of frequency preferences (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2010; Rothschild et al., 2010; Panniello et al., 2018; Romero et al., 2020; Winkowski and Kanold, 2013; Tischbirek et al., 2019), and here we show that ferret A1 shares the same spatial organization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing ferrets to prior mouse studies.

claim: The complexity of frequency receptive fields can account for much of the local heterogeneity in both mice and ferrets.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that the complexity of frequency receptive fields can account for much of the local heterogeneity in both mice and ferrets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in both species.

claim: The locally heterogeneous sensory maps described in primary cortical areas may be a consequence of complex stimulus feature extraction.
source: Thus, the locally heterogeneous sensory maps described in primary cortical areas may be a consequence of complex stimulus feature extraction.
evidence: This is a conclusion and interpretation drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Electrophysiological and widefield imaging studies have described a tonotopic gradient in the primary auditory cortex of all mammalian species studied, including humans.
source: Electrophysiological and widefield imaging studies have described a tonotopic gradient in the primary auditory cortex of all mammalian species studied, including humans (Romani et al., 1982), monkeys (Merzenich and Brugge, 1973), cats (Hind, 1953), ferrets (Kelly et al., 1986a), gerbils (Steffen et al., 1988), rats (Sally and Kelly, 1988) and mice (Stiebler et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: This global tonotopic organization has been confirmed in two-photon calcium imaging studies of primary auditory cortex in mice and marmosets.
source: This global tonotopic organization has been confirmed in two-photon calcium imaging studies of primary auditory cortex in mice (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2010; Rothschild et al., 2010; Romero et al., 2020; Winkowski and Kanold, 2013; Tischbirek et al., 2019; Issa et al., 2014) and marmosets (Zeng et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: This is the first two-photon calcium imaging of auditory cortex in carnivores.
source: Here, we performed the first two-photon calcium imaging of auditory cortex in carnivores, and show that this result generalizes to ferrets.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study.

claim: The stereotyped position of ferret A1 within reliable anatomical landmarks allowed combining data from multiple animals onto a template of A1.
source: The stereotyped position of ferret A1 within reliable anatomical landmarks allowed us to combine data from multiple animals onto a template of A1, as in previous electrophysiological studies (Bizley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by a citation.

claim: The combined ferret A1 map showed a clear dorsal-to-ventral tonotopic gradient for neurons with single-peaked, double-peaked and, to a lesser extent, complex frequency receptive fields.
source: This map showed a clear dorsal-to-ventral tonotopic gradient for neurons with single-peaked, double-peaked and, to a lesser extent, complex frequency receptive fields.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claim: There was no systematic spatial arrangement of the second frequency peak in double-peaked neurons.
source: In contrast, we observed no systematic spatial arrangement of the second frequency peak, or in the difference between frequency peaks in double-peaked neurons.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claim: There was no systematic spatial arrangement of the difference between frequency peaks in double-peaked neurons.
source: In contrast, we observed no systematic spatial arrangement of the second frequency peak, or in the difference between frequency peaks in double-peaked neurons.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claim: Global tonotopy is the main spatial organizational principle in primary auditory cortex.
source: Together, these findings support the well-established idea that global tonotopy is the main spatial organizational principle in primary auditory cortex, and is observed within all neurons that are frequency sensitive.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and established knowledge.

claim: In both ferrets and mice, neurons with single-peaked FRAs were organized homogeneously, with almost 90% of them in a given imaging field presenting BFs within the expected frequency range.
source: In both ferrets and mice, neurons with single-peaked FRAs were organized homogeneously, with almost 90% of them in a given imaging field presenting BFs within the expected frequency range, assuming a tonotopic gradient of < 4.9 oct/mm in mice and 2.9 oct/mm in ferrets.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data in both species.

claim: Signal correlation analysis confirmed local tonotopic organization, as proximate neurons were more similarly tuned than distant ones within an imaging field.
source: Signal correlation analysis further confirmed local tonotopic organization, as proximate neurons were more similarly tuned than distant ones within an imaging field (~250 μm2).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Double-peaked neurons were less ordered, with ~ 60% of their BFs within the expected range and greater local variability around the global tonotopic gradient, compared to single-peaked neurons.
source: Double-peaked neurons were less ordered, with ~ 60% of their BFs within the expected range and greater local variability around the global tonotopic gradient, compared to single-peaked neurons.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claim: Only 30% of complex neurons in a given imaging field were within the expected BF range.
source: In contrast to single- and double-peaked neurons, only 30% of complex neurons in a given imaging field were within the expected BF range, and their signal correlations were lower and less spatially dependent.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claim: The signal correlations of complex neurons were lower and less spatially dependent than single- and double-peaked neurons.
source: In contrast to single- and double-peaked neurons, only 30% of complex neurons in a given imaging field were within the expected BF range, and their signal correlations were lower and less spatially dependent.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claim: Romero et al. have recently shown that BFs are more locally variable among neurons with poorly-defined frequency tuning.
source: Previous studies have identified multi-peaked neurons in the A1 of mice (Winkowski and Kanold, 2013), rats (Turner et al., 2005), cats (Sutter and Schreiner, 1991) and marmosets (Kadia and Wang, 2003), and Romero et al. have recently shown that BFs are more locally variable among neurons with poorly-defined frequency tuning (Romero et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The association between frequency receptive field complexity and tonotopy was remarkably similar for mice and ferrets.
source: The association between frequency receptive field complexity and tonotopy was remarkably similar for mice and ferrets, suggesting that this may be a common feature of the mammalian cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing mice and ferrets.

claim: The complexity of receptive fields may explain the observed local variability of orientation tuning in V1 and whisker preferences in barrel cortex.
source: The complexity of receptive fields may also explain the observed local variability of orientation tuning in V1 (Bonin et al., 2011; Andermann et al., 2013) and whisker preferences in barrel cortex (Kerr et al., 2007; Sato et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative statement drawing on the current findings and prior research.

claim: The departure from strict tonotopy in A1, compared to earlier processing stations, may be an unavoidable result of complex spectrotemporal processing.
source: The departure from strict tonotopy in A1, compared to earlier processing stations, such as the central nucleus of the inferior colliculus (Barnstedt et al., 2015), may in fact be an unavoidable result of complex spectrotemporal processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the findings and prior research.

claim: Noise correlations were lower within local populations of complex neurons than within single- and double-peaked neurons.
source: We found that noise correlations were lower within local populations of complex neurons than within single- and double-peaked neurons.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claim: Neurons with complex frequency responses may receive inputs from neurons in more distant regions of the tonotopic map.
source: Those with complex frequency responses, on the other hand, may receive inputs from neurons in more distant regions of the tonotopic gradient.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: In V1, synaptic connections are more probable among neurons with similar orientation tuning.
source: In V1, synaptic connections are more probable among neurons with similar orientation tuning (Cossell et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A1 neurons with simple frequency tuning may have stronger local connections to similarly tuned neurons, supporting well-defined tonotopy.
source: From our experiments, we might expect A1 neurons with simple frequency tuning to have stronger local connections to similarly tuned neurons, supporting well-defined tonotopy.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings and analogy to V1.

claim: An equivalent tonotopic organization of well-tuned neurons exists in ferrets and mice, despite the fact that the A1 of ferrets represents ~ 3 oct/mm, while that of mice represents ~ 5 oct/mm.
source: Our results show that an equivalent tonotopic organization of well-tuned neurons exists in ferrets and mice, despite the fact that the A1 of ferrets represents ~ 3 oct/mm, while that of mice represents ~ 5 oct/mm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing mice and ferrets.

claim: Local heterogeneity in the tonotopic map is unlikely to be due to limitations in brain size, or other potential factors that are inherent to rodents.
source: Thus, local heterogeneity in the tonotopic map is unlikely to be due to limitations in brain size, or other potential factors that are inherent to rodents.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing mice and ferrets.

claim: Zeng et al., 2019 recently reported that BFs of A1 neurons are more locally variable in rats than in marmosets.
source: In contrast to this view, Zeng et al., 2019 recently reported that BFs of A1 neurons are more locally variable in rats than in marmosets.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The marmoset cortex may contain a smoother tonotopic arrangement than other species studied.
source: It is possible that the marmoset cortex contains a smoother tonotopic arrangement than other species studied, and this would be consistent with the high number of single-peaked neurons presented in their study (Zeng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of prior research findings.

claim: The reported difference between marmoset and rat A1 tonotopy might be accounted for if differences in the size of A1, complexity of frequency tuning, and hearing ranges of these two species are taken into consideration.
source: Alternatively, the reported difference between marmoset and rat A1 tonotopy might be accounted for if differences in the size of A1, complexity of frequency tuning, and hearing ranges of these two species are taken into consideration.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation offering an alternative explanation.

claim: Issa et al., 2014 reported more homogenous tonotopy in mouse A1 than other two-photon imaging studies.
source: Issa et al., 2014 reported more homogenous tonotopy in mouse A1 than other two-photon imaging studies (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2010; Rothschild et al., 2010; Panniello et al., 2018; Romero et al., 2020; Tischbirek et al., 2019), although the local variability in BF was still higher than that of marmosets (Zeng et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Both two-photon calcium imaging and single unit electrophysiological studies have demonstrated that there is little change in a neuron's BF between passively listening and anesthetized states.
source: Both two-photon calcium imaging (Romero et al., 2020; Tischbirek et al., 2019) and single unit electrophysiological studies (Guo et al., 2012) have demonstrated that there is little change in a neuron's BF between passively listening and anesthetized states, so this alone is unlikely to account for the smooth tonotopy observed by Issa et al., 2014.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neuropil signals contaminating neural responses can lead to smoother tonotopic maps.
source: Neuropil signals contaminating neural responses can lead to smoother tonotopic maps (Romero et al., 2020), on the other hand, as the signals in axons and dendrites are averaged across the local population.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research and represents an inference about methodological effects.

claim: Issa et al. used the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP3, which has a lower calcium sensitivity than GCaMP6.
source: Finally, Issa et al. used the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP3, which has a lower calcium sensitivity than GCaMP6.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in a prior study.

claim: The lower calcium sensitivity of GCaMP3 may have led to the detection of only the strongest variations in calcium influx, typically seen in single-peaked neurons.
source: This may have led to the detection of only the strongest variations in calcium influx, typically seen here in single-peaked neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about methodological effects.

claim: Fewer A1 neurons exhibited frequency sensitivity in ferrets (19%) than in mice (44%).
source: First, in both species, the majority of neurons were not sensitive to changes in tone frequency, but fewer A1 neurons exhibited frequency sensitivity in ferrets (19%) than in mice (44%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data comparing mice and ferrets.

claim: Most superficial A1 neurons do not respond to pure tones, especially in anesthetized animals.
source: While these numbers may seem low, most superficial A1 neurons do not even respond to pure tones, especially in anesthetized animals (Panniello et al., 2018; Tischbirek et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tonotopic maps do not reflect the spatial organization of response properties of most auditory cortical neurons.
source: Therefore, it is important to keep in mind that tonotopic maps do not reflect the spatial organization of response properties of most auditory cortical neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and prior research.

claim: The proportions of multi-peaked neurons in microelectrode recordings in ferret A1 are equivalent to those reported in marmoset A1 recordings.
source: In contrast, the proportions of multi-peaked neurons in our microelectrode recordings in ferret A1 are equivalent to those reported in marmoset A1 recordings (Kadia and Wang, 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's results to prior research.

claim: Neurons in ferret and marmoset A1 may be better suited to integrate information across frequency bands or encode more complex spectrotemporal features.
source: These results may indicate that neurons in ferret and marmoset A1 are better suited to integrate information across frequency bands or encode more complex spectrotemporal features.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Neurons with multiple frequency peaks would be useful for identifying sound sources based on their spectral timbre.
source: For example, neurons with multiple frequency peaks would be useful for identifying sound sources based on their spectral timbre (Bizley et al., 2009), or may provide harmonic templates for pitch perception (Feng and Wang, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential functions, supported by citations.

claim: Neurons with multiple frequency peaks may provide harmonic templates for pitch perception.
source: For example, neurons with multiple frequency peaks would be useful for identifying sound sources based on their spectral timbre (Bizley et al., 2009), or may provide harmonic templates for pitch perception (Feng and Wang, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential functions, supported by citations.

claim: Neurons in layers 2 and 3 of A1 differ in their morphology, connectivity and function.
source: While layers 2 and 3 are often regarded as a single processing unit, neurons in these two laminae of A1 differ in their morphology, connectivity and function (Atencio and Schreiner, 2010; Oviedo et al., 2010; Meng et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Most ferret imaging areas were likely located in layer 2, while calcium transients in mice were imaged in both layers 2 and 3.
source: In our study, most ferret imaging areas were likely located in layer 2 (based on their depth), while calcium transients in mice were imaged in both layers 2 and 3.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods and data.

claim: Meng et al reported that neurons in layer 2 have broader frequency tuning than those in layer 3.
source: For example, Meng et al reported that neurons in layer 2 have broader frequency tuning than those in layer 3 (Meng et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The potential laminar difference in imaging location could partially explain why neurons imaged in the mouse dataset had broader frequency tuning than the ferret data.
source: This potential laminar difference in imaging location could partially explain why neurons imaged in our mouse dataset had broader frequency tuning than our ferret data.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: With some exceptions, electrophysiological studies have typically reported smoother tonotopic gradients than two-photon imaging studies.
source: With some exceptions (Bizley et al., 2005), electrophysiological studies have typically reported smoother tonotopic gradients than two-photon imaging studies (Hackett et al., 2011; Stiebler et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Extracellular microelectrode recordings are more likely to detect and cluster neurons with higher firing rates.
source: Because extracellular microelectrode recordings are more likely to detect and cluster neurons with higher firing rates (Shoham et al., 2006), such studies may oversample neurons with single-peaked FRAs and therefore with more precise tonotopy.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents an inference about methodological effects.

claim: > 80% of frequency-sensitive neurons recorded from superficial A1 using microelectrodes had single-peaked FRAs: approximately double the proportion of single-peaked FRAs identified using two-photon calcium imaging in the same species.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that > 80% of frequency-sensitive neurons that we recorded from superficial A1 using microelectrodes had single-peaked FRAs: approximately double the proportion of single-peaked FRAs identified using two-photon calcium imaging in the same species.
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing two experimental methods.

claim: An electrophysiological study of marmoset auditory cortex found that 20% of neurons showed multi-peaked frequency tuning.
source: An electrophysiological study of marmoset auditory cortex also found that 20% of neurons showed multi-peaked frequency tuning (Kadia and Wang, 2003).
